books.section: Topic 1.5 Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System
The Social Structure of Spanish America
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

parts.modelAnswer: Peninsulares, Spaniards born in Spain, stood at the top of the hierarchy. Criollos, Spaniards born in the Americas, stood just below them.
parts.prompt: Identify one group that stood at the top of the casta hierarchy.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for naming one accurate top group, peninsulares or criollos.
scoring.notEarned: Naming mestizos or mulattos as the top group does not earn the point.

parts.modelAnswer: Spaniards were greatly outnumbered, and Spanish men greatly outnumbered Spanish women, so mixing was common. Each new combination of parents produced a new category, because the regime insisted on ranking everyone by ancestry.
parts.prompt: Explain why the casta system developed so many categories.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one accurate cause of the many categories, such as widespread mixing, or the regime's insistence on ranking by ancestry.
scoring.notEarned: Stating only that there were many categories, with no cause given, does not earn the point.

parts.modelAnswer: A person's ancestry fixed their legal and social status, deciding what offices they could hold and how they were treated. A mestizo or mulatto faced limits a peninsular never did.
parts.prompt: Explain one way the casta hierarchy affected a person's life in Spanish America.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one accurate effect, such as limits on office-holding, legal status, or social treatment.
scoring.notEarned: Stating only that the hierarchy ranked people, with no effect on a life explained, does not earn the point.

stimulus.text: Spanish colonizers developed an elaborate caste system in the New World. At the top stood peninsulares, Spaniards born in Spain, and criollos, Spaniards born in the Americas, who together made up only one or two percent of the population. Below them came mestizos, children of Spanish men and Indigenous women, then mulattos, children of Spanish men and African women, with American Indians and Africans at the bottom. The system recognized even finer gradations, based on the specific percentage of each lineage a person possessed.
